What is covered

Interior painting, in full

  • Walls, ceilings, trim, doors and window casings, priced separately so you can see what you are paying for
  • Patching, filling and sanding before anything is coated
  • Masking, floor protection and putting the room back
  • Color matching to what is already there, or a full change with the right primer under it
  • Closets, stairwells and hallways, which are the parts that get skipped

How the job runs

The order it happens in

  1. Walk-throughWe stand in the room, count the doors and the trim runs, and look at the condition of what is already on the wall. That is the only honest way to price it.
  2. PrepOur crew fills, patches, sands, caulks and masks. This is where the time goes on an older house and it is the part that decides whether the finish still looks right in five years.
  3. Prime where it is neededBare patches, stains, and any big color change get primed. Skipping this is how a job needs a third coat it was never priced for.
  4. Finish coatsWe cut in, roll out, then look at it in daylight and fix what daylight shows.
  5. Put it backFurniture back, hardware back, floors clear. We put the room back rather than leaving that to you.

What moves the number

Why two quotes for the same room can look nothing alike

No price is published here, because a real number needs somebody to stand in the room first. What can be published is what actually drives it, so you can read any quote you get and know what you are looking at.

  1. Condition, not square footageThis is the biggest variable and the least visible one. Patched drywall, old nicotine staining, chalking plaster and previously peeling enamel all add hours before a finish coat goes anywhere near the wall.
  2. Whether the color is changingTwo coats is the normal assumption. Going dark to light, or into any deep base color, is realistically three coats plus a tinted primer.
  3. Ceiling heightA two story entry or a vaulted room is a staging job, not a room job. It should never be quoted at the same rate as a bedroom.
  4. How much trim there isTwo houses with identical floor area can be very different jobs. A 1960s house with heavy casing, six panel doors and full baseboard runs is a lot of linear feet of cutting in, and trim is the line homeowners forget to ask about.
  5. Pre-1978 housingSee the note below. It is a real difference in setup and cleanup on a large share of the houses in this area.

Ask every contractor the same three questions

What preparation is included. How many coats. What happens to the price if the preparation turns out to be worse than it looks. The answers, more than the total, are what tell you which quote is real.

Questions

About interior painting

Do you paint ceilings and trim, or just walls?

All of it, and they are priced separately so you can decide. A lot of people ask for walls only, then look at the trim next to fresh paint and change their mind. It is worth asking for both numbers up front so that is a decision and not a surprise.

Can you match a color I already have?

Usually. Bring a chip off the wall, a switch plate or the old can and it can be matched at the paint counter. If the existing color has faded and a perfect match is not possible, you will be told that before the work starts, not after.

How many coats?

Two is normal over a similar color. A big change, a deep color or bare patched drywall needs primer and often a third coat. That gets settled at the walk-through so it is in the price rather than added later.

Do I need to move everything out?

No. Big furniture usually moves to the middle of the room and gets covered. Small, breakable and personal things are better off out of the way before anybody arrives.

My house is from the 1960s. Does that matter?

Yes, and it is worth understanding. The EPA lead renovation, repair and painting rule covers anyone paid to disturb painted surfaces in housing built before 1978. Median build year in Bridgeview is about 1975, Oak Lawn about 1967 and Burbank about 1965, so most of the houses here are inside it. Ask any contractor how they handle it. EPA guidance is here.
